extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers of probability, logic of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to form, measure, combine, and evaluate probabilistic belief from evidence; contrasts conceptualistic (a priori) probability with inductive/relative-frequency approaches and gives sampling-error rules. Includes practical examples (bean/urn sampling, census).

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief proportional to logarithm of chance
rubrics_metrics.description: The feeling (intensity) of belief ought to be the logarithm of the chance; as chance increases the feeling of belief increases and as chance diminishes the feeling of belief diminishes, reversing sign at an even chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: when independent arguments concur their chances multiply, so the measure of belief that adds under multiplication should be the logarithm. This choice accords with Fechner's psychophysical law (sensation proportional to logarithm of stimulus). Infinite chance corresponds to infinite belief; even chance corresponds to zero belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination rule (balancing reasons)
rubrics_metrics.description: For independent concurrent arguments, take the sum of the feelings of belief produced separately by all 'pro' arguments, subtract the sum for 'con' arguments, and the remainder is the feeling of belief we ought to have overall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a practical procedure often called 'balancing reasons' and follows from measuring belief on the logarithmic (additive) scale since independent chances multiply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability must be inferred on evidence (probability expresses a fact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability, to have any value, must express a fact and is therefore a thing to be inferred upon evidence rather than assigned arbitrarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating probabilities as mere abstract numbers divorced from empirical argument; probabilities should be connected to the state of knowledge and the available arguments/evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-number representation of belief (probability + knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: To express the proper state of our belief not one number but two are requisite: (1) the inferred probability and (2) the amount (or accuracy) of knowledge on which that probability is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: with few samples (small s) an even-looking probability should be accompanied by low confidence; with many samples the uncertainty part may vanish. When knowledge is slight the uncertainty component may overwhelm the point estimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of 'even chance' for total ignorance (critique of conceptualistic principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The conceptualistic principle that alternatives of which we know nothing should be considered equally probable (yielding an even chance like 1/2) is absurd because enumeration and choice of scale are arbitrary and can produce paradoxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated with color-chart and urn thought-experiments: assigning 1/2 to totally unknown continuous alternatives leads to contradictions (e.g., nested areas each assigned 1/2 would imply impossible totals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent arguments combine by multiplying chances
rubrics_metrics.description: When two arguments are entirely independent (neither weakening nor strengthening each other), the chances of their concurrence are to be multiplied to get the chance of their combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the basis for adopting an additive measure (logarithm) of belief because multiplying chances corresponds to adding logarithms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between analytic (deductive) and synthetic (inductive) reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: All reasonings are of two kinds: explicative/analytic/deductive and amplificative/synthetic/inductive. Analytic reasoning derives conclusions from facts laid down in the premises; synthetic reasoning goes beyond premises and provides genuine increase of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic inferences can have calculable probabilities (given premises); synthetic inferences cannot be reduced to analytic probability but rather are assessed by the trustworthiness of the inductive procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing inductive trustworthiness by relative frequency (start from fact and follow back)
rubrics_metrics.description: To know the probability that our conclusion will accord with fact, begin with the fact aimed at and follow back to the premises to see the proportion (relative frequency) of premises that would yield the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use urn/sampling analogies: although we cannot have an urn of universes, sampling and relative-frequency mathematics let us estimate how often synthetic inferences of a given type will be true within a degree of approximation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling error / probable error rules (approximate numerical guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given true proportion p and s draws, the probable error of the proportion obtained by induction scales with sqrt{p(1-p)/s}; numerical multipliers are given for confidence levels (e.g., half the time within 0.477×..., 9/10 within 1.163×..., 99/100 within 1.821×..., etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete use: with census numbers the text uses these multipliers to compute probable errors for proportions (example: male proportion 0.5082 among ~1,000,000 white children gives probable error ≈ 0.0003). The formulas allow judging whether observed differences can be attributed to chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edge-case probabilities (very large or very small p give more secure inductions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the real value of the probability sought inductively is either very large or very small, the inductive reasoning is more secure (smaller relative sampling error for given sample size).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if true proportion is 1 white in 100 and you draw 100 times, probabilities of 0,1,2,... white draws are such that you'll be tolerably certain of not being in error by more than one ball in 100.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction principle: similar conditions yield similar experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Synthetic inference is founded upon a classification of facts by the manner of obtaining them: a number of facts obtained in a given way will in general resemble other facts obtained in the same way; experiences whose conditions are the same will have the same general characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle—that processes under similar conditions tend to produce similar results—is the practical rule underlying successful induction and justifies trusting inductive procedures in the long run.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful probability pertains to our single world (not all possible worlds)
rubrics_metrics.description: We should be interested in the probability that our conclusion will accord with the fact in the world we inhabit, not the proportion of all possible worlds in which the conclusion holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This motivates the shift from abstract 'probability of fact given all possible states' to relative-frequency estimates of trustworthiness of our inductive methods with respect to our actual conditions.
